meta.location: Jershon and the borders of Zarahemla
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Two griefs told apart by hope

world_behind.title: The armies were already in place
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has the Nephite forces set around Jershon and the borders, exactly as the vote in Alma 27 promised. The protection was arranged before the enemy arrived.

world_behind.title: The Lamanite army followed the refugees
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says they came after their brethren into the wilderness. The battle happens because the Nephites kept a promise about people who would not fight.

world_behind.title: Mormon dates the battle against the whole record
world_behind.text: Verse 2 calls it the largest since Lehi left Jerusalem, a span of roughly six hundred years of his own sources. He is measuring against everything he has read.

world_behind.title: Both sides lose heavily
world_behind.text: Verse 2 gives tens of thousands of Lamanites; verse 3 says the slaughter among the Nephites was tremendous too. The victory in this chapter is expensive on the page where it is reported.

world_behind.title: The mourning is listed by relationship
world_behind.text: Verse 5 pairs each mourner with the one lost, wife to husband and parent to child. Mormon writes the grief as a roll of who lost whom.

world_behind.title: Verses 7 through 9 are a closing note
world_behind.text: They end the fifteenth year, summarize the account of Ammon and his brethren, and bless them. The record marks the seam where the flashback rejoins the main line.

world_behind.title: The fifteen-year total is the real subject
world_behind.text: Verses 10 and 11 count from the first year of the judges: many thousand lives, bodies in the earth and bodies in heaps. Alma 1 through 28 is being audited in three verses.

words.text: Formal, voiced grief. Treated at Mosiah 21:9. The record uses it eight times and the King James Bible twenty-five, where it names a genre as much as an emotion. Mormon pairs it with mourning to describe a whole country making the same sound at once.

A state of gravity, and in the King James Bible a kept observance. It appears once in the record, and twice in the Bible. Mormon uses it of a day given over to fasting and prayer after a battle, which turns national grief into something observed.

Beyond taking in. The word appears once in scripture. Mormon attaches it to the joy of Ammon and his brethren, in the same sentence as their sufferings and sorrows and afflictions, and it is the only item on the list he says he cannot measure.

Decaying, crumbling. The record uses it twice: here, of bodies in heaps after this battle, and in Mormon 6, where Moroni says the same of the bodies at Cumorah and then promises they will become incorruptible. The word carries the record's two largest fields of dead.
To leap for joy. It occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it of people who are mourning at the same time. He needs a strong word for the joy and a separate clause for the grief.

Unevenness, disparity. Treated at Alma 16:16. The word appears six times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Alma 4 and Mosiah 29 use it of wealth and rank among the living; here Mormon uses it of the difference between two sets of dead.

phrases.term: Such an one as never had been known among all the people in the land from the time Lehi left Jerusalem
phrases.text: Mormon reaches back six hundred years to size the battle. He has the whole record in front of him when he writes it, which makes the claim an editorial judgment rather than a witness report.

phrases.term: The cry of widows mourning for their husbands
phrases.text: The first item in a list of four relationships. Mormon starts with the women who are left, and the verse works through the household until every position has someone missing from it.

phrases.term: A time of much fasting and prayer
phrases.text: The country's response to the losses, given in seven words. Mormon records what the people did with the sorrowful day, and the answer is that they kept it.

Two words closing the account of a fourteen-year mission. Mormon has just listed journeyings, sufferings, sorrows, and afflictions, and he puts the joy in the same sentence and marks it as the part he cannot get his arms around.

phrases.term: The bodies of many thousands are moldering in heaps upon the face of the earth
phrases.text: Unburied dead, fifteen years of them. Mormon writes it in the present tense, as a description of the land as it stands, and the sentence continues into what the survivors have reason to fear.

phrases.term: They rejoice and exult in the hope, and even know
phrases.text: Mormon distinguishes two griefs by what the mourners can say about the dead. He grants the second group hope and then upgrades it to knowledge in the same clause, on the strength of the promises of the Lord.

phrases.term: How great the inequality of man is because of sin and transgression
phrases.text: The conclusion he draws from the two kinds of funeral. Everyone in both groups is dead; what differs is what their families can expect, and Mormon calls that difference an inequality with a named cause.

phrases.term: The cunning plans which he hath devised to ensnare the hearts of men
phrases.text: Mormon names the devil's method as planning. The word cunning attaches to design rather than to force, and the target is hearts, which is where Alma 27 said Satan had his hold on the Amalekites.

phrases.term: The great call of diligence of men to labor in the vineyards of the Lord
phrases.text: The chapter ends by turning the arithmetic into an assignment. Having counted the dead and sorted the mourners, Mormon says what the living should be doing, and Alma 29 opens with Alma wishing he could do more of it.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The place name is repeated until it encircles
verses.text: Jershon stands three times in the opening sentence: the people of Ammon are established there, a church is established there, and the armies of the Nephites "were set round about the land of Jershon." The sentence does with repetition what the armies do with position, and the verse closes on the Lamanites arriving.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: The largest battle in the record takes forty-three words
verses.text: It is "such an one as never had been known among all the people in the land from the time Lehi left Jerusalem," and tens of thousands fall. The record makes the superlative claim and then stops. No commander is named, no manoeuvre described, no ground given or taken.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: The year is closed twice, with a blessing in between
verses.text: "And thus endeth the fifteenth year" at verse 7; "the fifteenth year of the reign of the judges is ended" at verse 9. Between the two endings Mormon files two summaries naming what he has just abridged, and interrupts the first with something a table of contents does not usually carry: "And now may the Lord, the Redeemer of all men, bless their souls forever." The editor prays inside his own index.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: One phrase counts four different things
verses.text: Many thousands falls in verses 10, 11 and 12, and lands five times across them: the lives destroyed, the bodies in the earth, the bodies moldering in heaps, the mourners who fear, and the mourners who hope. The same measure is applied to the dead and to the living, and the only thing that separates the last two groups is what they expect, not what they have lost.

verses.label: v. 13–14
verses.title: The moral formula fires three times in two verses
verses.text: "And thus we see" opens verse 13 and is used twice more in verse 14. The record has just declined to explain a battle, and now supplies three conclusions in a row: the inequality of man, the call to labor, and the double reason for sorrow and rejoicing. What it withholds from the war it spends on the lesson.

chapter.title: A promise kept costs tens of thousands of lives
chapter.text: The Nephites voted in Alma 27 to guard people who would not fight, and Alma 28 is the invoice. Mormon puts the vote and the battle in adjacent chapters without drawing the moral.

chapter.title: The largest battle in six hundred years gets three verses
chapter.text: Two for the fighting, one for the outcome. Mormon spends the rest of the chapter on the mourning, which tells the reader what he thinks the event actually was.

chapter.title: Grief is written as a household roll
chapter.text: Widows, fathers, daughters, brothers. Nobody in verse 5 is named, and every one of them is identified by the person they lost.

chapter.title: The record stops to bless its own subjects
chapter.text: Verse 8 asks the Redeemer to bless the souls of Ammon and his brethren forever. Mormon rarely speaks to God inside a summary, and he does it here at the end of their story.

chapter.title: Fifteen years are counted at once
chapter.text: The chapter reaches back over Alma 1 through 27 and totals the dead. Individual wars that read as episodes become a single running loss when they are added up.

chapter.title: Two funerals, one difference
chapter.text: Verses 11 and 12 set two groups of mourners side by side and use the same number for both, "many thousands." The bodies are equally dead in both verses. What differs is one clause: the first group mourn "because they have reason to fear, according to the promises of the Lord, that they are consigned to a state of endless wo," and the second "rejoice and exult in the hope, and even know... that they are raised to dwell at the right hand of God." Verse 13 names the difference, "the inequality of man," and locates its cause in sin rather than in death.

chapter.title: The devil is described as a planner
chapter.text: Cunning plans devised to ensnare hearts. Force does not appear in the description; the whole account of the opposition in verse 13 is design and patience.

chapter.title: The chapter ends on work
chapter.text: After the count and the diagnosis, Mormon's conclusion is that laborers are needed. Alma 29 begins with a man who wants to be a bigger laborer than he is.

applications.title: Keep the promise when the bill comes
applications.text: The Nephites had undertaken at Alma 27:23 to defend the people of Ammon, and this chapter is what that cost: "a tremendous battle; yea, even such an one as never had been known among all the people in the land from the time Lehi left Jerusalem." An agreement is tested by the year it turns expensive.

applications.title: Name who lost whom
applications.text: Mormon writes the grief by relationship rather than by number, "the cry of widows mourning for their husbands, and also of fathers mourning for their sons, and the daughter for the brother, yea, the brother for the father." When you record a loss, name the ties that were broken.

applications.title: Keep the sorrowful day
applications.text: A whole country stopped, "a time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer." Marking a bad thing with an occasion, rather than pressing on, is treated here as the appropriate response and not as weakness.

applications.title: Report both accounts in the same paragraph
applications.text: Verse 8 sums the mission with its "sufferings... sorrows, and their afflictions, and their incomprehensible joy," and verse 9 sums the wars. The same year holds both, and the record refuses to let either one be the whole story.

applications.title: Notice what makes the two funerals different
applications.text: Two groups of thousands mourn, and the difference is not in the deaths but in what the living can know: some "have reason to fear," and others "rejoice and exult in the hope, and even know." Ask what you would actually know if you were standing on either side.

applications.title: Call the difference by its name
applications.text: Mormon calls it "the inequality of man" and locates the cause in sin and in the devil's cunning plans. Naming an unevenness and naming its cause are different acts, and this verse does both in a sentence.

applications.title: Draw two conclusions, not one
applications.text: The chapter's summary holds them together, "the great reason of sorrow, and also of rejoicing." A response to a year like this that has only one emotional register in it is leaving something out.

applications.title: Do the work you can do
applications.text: The chapter that counts the dead ends on "the great call of diligence of men to labor in the vineyards of the Lord." The answer offered to a season of loss is a task rather than an explanation.

questions.text: What have I set in place before it was needed, and what am I still leaving until it is?
What victory of mine cost other people something I have not counted?
Who in my life is mourning right now, and do I know the relationship?
When did I last stop and mark something instead of pushing through?
What joy in my life would I call incomprehensible?
What do I actually know about the people I have lost?
Which part of the vineyard is mine, and am I in it?

entries.reason: the promise being kept, made by vote one chapter earlier

targets.quote: we will set our armies between the land Jershon and the land Nephi,
targets.verse_text: And behold, we will set our armies between the land Jershon and the land Nephi, that we may protect our brethren in the land Jershon; and this we do for our brethren, on account of their fear to take up arms against their brethren lest they should commit sin; and this their great fear came because of their sore repentance which they had, on account of their many murders and their awful wickedness.
